nodes.label: Mailbox
nodes.rationale: One FIFO queue of envelopes per actor; the dispatcher hands one envelope at a time to onReceive and waits, which is what makes the one-message-at-a-time guarantee physically true.

nodes.label: Unbounded FIFO is the default
nodes.rationale: Between v0.10 and v0.15 the default was bounded at 10 000 with drop-head, and the trade did not hold: the ceiling was not real (only the user queue was bounded, system messages were never capped) and a mailbox cannot tell what it is discarding — a delivery confirmation or a WebSocket close went through the same queue as telemetry, each turning into a filed defect. Loss is now something you ask for per actor, and growth is reported at 10 000 messages and each doubling.

nodes.label: BoundedMailbox
nodes.rationale: Constructing one yourself defaults to reject, because you built a bound and nothing else can be assumed about what is safe to lose; withMailboxOverflow defaults to drop-head, the policy that suits the workloads people reach for a bound to protect.

nodes.label: PriorityMailbox
nodes.rationale: Lower numbers first, ties by FIFO insertion. Sorted-insertion array today — O(log n) locate plus O(n) splice per enqueue — open to a heap-backed swap if a sustained 10 000-message backlog shows it in profiles.

nodes.label: Overflow policies (drop-head / drop-new / reject)
nodes.rationale: drop-head means freshest wins (telemetry), drop-new means first wins (command streams where reordering is unacceptable), reject means the sender deals with it — and reject throws at the tell call site, so B's overflowing mailbox surfaces as A restarting, which confuses triage.

nodes.label: drop-lowest-priority (and why not drop-head)
nodes.rationale: On a FIFO queue drop-head means discard the stalest, which works because arrival order is the only order; on a priority queue the head is the message priorityFor called most important, so dropping it would defeat the reason you chose the mailbox.

nodes.label: enqueueSignal obligation
nodes.rationale: The contract is queue it whatever your bound says. The base implementation delegates to your enqueue, correct for a queue that discards nothing and wrong for one that sheds — so override it whenever you override enqueue to shed. Delegating rather than writing to the base queue is deliberate: an envelope hidden in a store your dequeueUser never reads is worse than one you dropped.

nodes.label: undroppable envelope flag
nodes.rationale: Read by removeOldest, so a drop-head-shaped bound built on that seam steps over it for free without having to know why. Undroppable is not queue-jumping — it keeps its place in line and merely cannot be discarded from it.

nodes.label: DropReportingMailbox / observeDrops
nodes.rationale: Registration is additive, so your own onDrop keeps firing alongside the stock counter.

nodes.label: System messages always come first
nodes.rationale: Two queues live side by side and system messages have absolute precedence — which is why supervision reacts instantly. ref.stop() does not jump the queue: PoisonPill is a user message, making stop a graceful drain-then-stop, and a death-watch Terminated is a user message for the same reason — it must arrive after everything already told to the watcher.

nodes.label: priorityFor callback
nodes.rationale: An unrankable answer queues at the lowest priority rather than the highest — a priority that could not be determined must not outrank one that was stated — and the failure is contained rather than thrown, because priorityFor runs inside the sender tell and a sender is a bystander to the receiver mailbox configuration. Note the framework calls it with PoisonPill and Kill, which have no fields.

nodes.label: onPriorityError hook
nodes.rationale: Nothing else in the system reports a contained failure. Record and return — the hook runs on the sender stack too, so a throw from inside it puts the escape back.

nodes.label: RingBuffer-backed queues
nodes.rationale: A queue with no ceiling has to stay cheap when it is deep: taking the next message advances an index instead of reindexing everything behind it, so delivering one message does not cost more as the backlog grows.

nodes.label: ActorOptions.withMailbox(factory)
nodes.rationale: Called once per actor instance including on restart, so each restarted actor gets a fresh empty queue. It replaces rather than configures, so combining it with withMailboxCapacity is a configuration error rather than a silent precedence rule; never return a shared instance from two factories.

nodes.label: withMailboxCapacity / withMailboxOverflow
nodes.rationale: Capacity is what creates the bound; a policy without a capacity is rejected rather than silently ignored, since an unbounded mailbox never overflows. There is no system-wide mailbox setting — every bound is chosen per actor.

nodes.label: actor_mailbox_* metrics
nodes.rationale: actor_mailbox_dropped_total is labelled by actor class and policy, not per actor — shedding is what a bounded mailbox is for, so a per-actor label would mint a permanent series for every actor behaving as designed. actor_mailbox_wait_seconds climbs as soon as an actor stops keeping up; actor_mailbox_depth p99 is what to size a capacity from.

nodes.label: Unstash goes through prependUser
nodes.rationale: PriorityMailbox re-runs the priority function rather than pushing to the front, so unstashAll goes through the same enqueue path and therefore the same bound — replaying the stash on a full bounded priority mailbox can discard messages. BoundedMailbox unstash bypasses the bound instead.

hyperedges.label: The undroppable lane no mailbox bound may shed
